description: This topic covers the meaning of pasture and fodder, types of pastures, common pasture grasses and legumes, fodder crops, fodder conservation through hay and silage, grazing systems, and the importance of good pasture management for livestock.

mcq.questionText: What is the meaning of the term 'pasture'?

options.text: Land covered with grasses and legumes used for grazing livestock
A building where animals are kept at night
A machine used to cut grass for animals
A type of fertilizer applied to crops

mcq.explanation: Pasture is land covered mainly with grasses and legumes that livestock graze on directly.

mcq.questionText: Which of the following best describes fodder?

options.text: Wild fruits eaten by animals in the bush
Crops grown, cut and carried to feed livestock
Salt licks placed in the field for cattle
Water provided to animals during the dry season

mcq.explanation: Fodder refers to crops that are grown, harvested and carried to the animals rather than being grazed directly.

mcq.questionText: A pasture that grows on its own without being planted by people is called a:

options.text: Sown pasture
Established pasture
Natural pasture
Artificial pasture

mcq.explanation: Natural pasture develops naturally without human planting, unlike sown or established pasture.

mcq.questionText: Which of the following is an established (sown) pasture?

options.text: Grass that grows by itself along the roadside
A field deliberately planted with Rhodes grass for grazing
A natural grassland in a game reserve
Weeds growing in an abandoned farm

mcq.explanation: An established pasture is one that the farmer deliberately plants with selected grasses or legumes such as Rhodes grass.

mcq.questionText: Which of the following is a common pasture grass in Tanzania?

options.text: Rhodes grass
Centro
Desmodium
Lucerne

mcq.explanation: Rhodes grass is a common pasture grass, while centro, desmodium and lucerne are pasture legumes.

mcq.questionText: Which of the following is a pasture legume?

options.text: Guinea grass
Napier grass
Lucerne
Star grass

mcq.explanation: Lucerne (alfalfa) is a pasture legume, while guinea, Napier and star grass are pasture grasses.

mcq.questionText: Why are pasture legumes important in a mixed pasture?

options.text: They make the pasture grow taller than grasses
They fix nitrogen in the soil and provide protein-rich feed
They prevent grasses from being eaten by animals
They reduce the amount of water needed by the pasture

mcq.explanation: Legumes fix atmospheric nitrogen through their root nodules, improving soil fertility, and are high in protein.

mcq.questionText: Which fodder crop is widely grown and cut to feed dairy cattle?

options.text: Napier grass
Sisal
Cotton
Coffee

mcq.explanation: Napier grass (elephant grass) is a popular fodder crop cut and carried to feed dairy cattle.

options.text: Green fodder stored in an airtight pit
Grass or legumes cut and dried for storage as animal feed
Fresh grass grazed directly by animals
Crop residues burnt in the field

mcq.explanation: Hay is forage that is cut and dried to a low moisture content so it can be stored for feeding during the dry season.

options.text: Dried grass stored in a barn
Green fodder preserved by fermentation in an airtight condition
Concentrate feed made from cereals
Mineral supplement given to cattle

mcq.explanation: Silage is succulent fodder preserved by fermentation under airtight (anaerobic) conditions, usually in a silo or pit.

mcq.questionText: Which condition is most important for making good silage?

options.text: Plenty of air must reach the fodder
Air must be excluded so fermentation can take place
The fodder must be completely dry before storage
The fodder must be exposed to direct sunlight

mcq.explanation: Silage making requires airtight (anaerobic) conditions so that fermentation, not rotting, preserves the fodder.

mcq.questionText: In which grazing system is land divided into paddocks and animals moved from one to another?

options.text: Continuous grazing
Rotational grazing
Zero grazing
Free grazing

mcq.explanation: In rotational grazing the pasture is divided into paddocks and animals are moved between them to allow grass to recover.

mcq.questionText: Which is an advantage of rotational grazing over continuous grazing?

options.text: It allows the pasture time to regrow and reduces overgrazing
It needs no fencing or paddocks at all
It allows animals to graze the same spot forever
It increases the spread of internal parasites

mcq.explanation: Rotational grazing rests each paddock in turn, allowing regrowth, reducing overgrazing and helping control parasites.

mcq.questionText: What is a likely result of overgrazing a pasture?

options.text: Improved soil fertility and thicker grass cover
Soil erosion and reduced pasture productivity
Faster regrowth of grasses
Higher milk yield from all animals

mcq.explanation: Overgrazing removes the protective grass cover, exposing soil to erosion and lowering the pasture's productivity.

mcq.questionText: A farmer wants to preserve surplus green Napier grass during the wet season for use in the dry season, but the weather is too rainy and cloudy for drying. Which conservation method is most suitable?

options.text: Making hay by spreading the grass in the sun
Making silage in an airtight pit
Leaving the grass standing in the field
Burning the grass to store the ash

mcq.explanation: Hay needs dry sunny weather, so during a rainy season silage making, which does not depend on sun drying, is more suitable.

fib.questionText: Land covered with grasses and legumes on which livestock graze is called _____.
fib.explanation: Pasture is grazing land covered mainly with grasses and legumes.

fib.questionText: Crops that are grown, cut and carried to feed livestock are known as _____.
fib.explanation: Fodder is cut-and-carried feed rather than feed grazed directly in the field.

fib.questionText: A pasture that grows naturally without being planted by people is called a _____ pasture.
fib.explanation: Natural pastures grow on their own without human planting.

fib.questionText: A pasture that a farmer deliberately plants with selected grasses and legumes is called an established or _____ pasture.
fib.explanation: Established pastures are also called sown pastures because they are planted by the farmer.

fib.questionText: Napier grass, which is cut and carried to feed dairy cattle, is also commonly known as _____ grass.
fib.explanation: Napier grass is also called elephant grass.

fib.questionText: Forage that is cut and dried for storage as animal feed is called _____.
fib.explanation: Hay is dried forage stored for use during feed shortages.

fib.questionText: Green fodder preserved by fermentation under airtight conditions is called _____.
fib.explanation: Silage is fermented, succulent fodder stored without air.

fib.questionText: A pit or structure in which silage is made and stored is called a _____.
fib.explanation: Silage is stored in a silo, which keeps out air to allow fermentation.

fib.questionText: The grazing system in which the pasture is divided into paddocks and animals are moved between them is called _____ grazing.
fib.explanation: Rotational grazing rests paddocks in turn to allow grass to recover.

fib.questionText: Pasture legumes are valuable because their root nodules fix _____ from the air, improving soil fertility.
fib.explanation: Legumes fix atmospheric nitrogen through bacteria in their root nodules.

tf.questionText: Pasture is land covered with grasses and legumes used for grazing livestock.
tf.explanation: This is the correct meaning of pasture.

tf.questionText: Fodder is feed that animals graze directly from the field.
tf.explanation: Fodder is cut and carried to animals; feed grazed directly is from pasture.

tf.questionText: Natural pasture is deliberately planted by the farmer with selected species.
tf.explanation: Natural pasture grows on its own; planted pasture is called established or sown pasture.

tf.questionText: Rhodes grass and Napier grass are examples of pasture and fodder grasses.
tf.explanation: Both are grasses used as feed for livestock.

tf.questionText: Lucerne and desmodium are pasture legumes.
tf.explanation: Lucerne and desmodium are legumes used in pastures.

tf.questionText: Hay is made by drying grass or legumes to a low moisture content.
tf.explanation: Hay is dried forage suitable for long storage.

tf.questionText: Silage is made by drying fodder in direct sunlight.
tf.explanation: Silage is preserved by fermentation under airtight conditions, not by sun drying; that describes hay.

tf.questionText: Continuous grazing keeps animals on the same pasture all the time without resting it.
tf.explanation: In continuous grazing animals graze the same area continuously with no rest period.

tf.questionText: Overgrazing improves the productivity of a pasture.
tf.explanation: Overgrazing damages the grass cover, encourages erosion and reduces pasture productivity.

tf.questionText: Good pasture management helps provide cheap and reliable feed that improves livestock health and production.
tf.explanation: Well-managed pastures supply nutritious, low-cost feed, supporting better animal health and output.

summary.correctAnswer: Land covered with grasses and legumes used for grazing livestock.
summary.explanation: Animals feed directly on the growing plants.

summary.correctAnswer: Crops grown, cut and carried to feed livestock.
summary.explanation: Fodder is fed to animals rather than grazed in place.

summary.correctAnswer: Natural pasture grows on its own, while established (sown) pasture is planted by the farmer.
summary.explanation: Established pastures use selected, productive species.

summary.correctAnswer: Examples include Rhodes grass, guinea grass, star grass and Napier grass.
summary.explanation: Grasses form the bulk of energy in pasture feed.

summary.correctAnswer: Examples include lucerne, desmodium, centro and clover.
summary.explanation: Legumes add protein and fix nitrogen in the soil.

summary.correctAnswer: They fix nitrogen to improve soil fertility and provide protein-rich feed.
summary.explanation: Nitrogen fixation occurs in their root nodules.

summary.correctAnswer: Hay is forage cut and dried for storage as feed during dry periods.
summary.explanation: Drying lowers moisture so the feed keeps without rotting.

summary.correctAnswer: Silage is green fodder preserved by fermentation under airtight conditions in a silo.
summary.explanation: Excluding air allows fermentation to preserve the fodder.

summary.correctAnswer: Rotational grazing moves animals between paddocks to rest pasture, while continuous grazing uses one area without rest.
summary.explanation: Rotation reduces overgrazing and controls parasites.

summary.correctAnswer: It provides cheap, nutritious and reliable feed that improves livestock health and production.
summary.explanation: It also conserves soil and prevents overgrazing.

hoq.questionText: A farmer notices that part of his grazing land has bare, eroded soil and very short grass, while a fenced section rested for some weeks has tall, healthy grass. What does this difference best demonstrate?

options.text: That continuous grazing without rest leads to overgrazing and soil erosion
That legumes always grow taller than grasses
That hay is better than silage for feeding
That natural pastures cannot support livestock

hoq.explanation: The bare eroded area shows the effect of continuous overgrazing, while the rested paddock shows the benefit of allowing regrowth as in rotational grazing.

hoq.questionText: Two farmers store equal amounts of fodder; one as hay and one as silage. After heavy rains leak into both stores, the hay becomes mouldy quickly but the silage in the sealed pit is less affected. Why does this happen?

options.text: Hay depends on low moisture, so added water spoils it, while sealed silage is already a moist, fermented, airtight product
Silage contains no nutrients, so water cannot spoil it
Hay is made from legumes only and silage from grasses only
Water always improves the quality of stored fodder

hoq.explanation: Hay is preserved by keeping it dry, so extra moisture encourages mould, whereas silage is preserved by fermentation in airtight conditions and tolerates moisture better when sealed.

hoq.questionText: A dairy farmer wants to lower feed costs and improve both the protein content of the feed and the fertility of the pasture soil. Which management decision best achieves all of these goals?

options.text: Plant only one type of grass and add chemical fertilizer every week
Establish a mixed pasture of grasses and legumes and use rotational grazing
Allow continuous grazing on bare land throughout the year
Stop growing pasture and rely only on bought concentrates

hoq.explanation: A grass-legume mixture adds protein and fixes nitrogen to enrich the soil, while rotational grazing keeps the pasture productive and feed costs low.
